title: Starters, Plenaries and Quick Checks
summary: Build a bank of twelve starters and ten plenaries, learn how to check understanding during the lesson, and set up vocabulary routines that keep new words alive.

p: A starter is the first activity. It should take five to eight minutes. Use these rules.
• It uses English from the first second.
• It needs very little preparation.
• It links to the last lesson or to today's topic.
• It is active: students write, speak, move or decide.
• It changes. Use different starters each week.
• It tells you something: who is ready, who forgot the last lesson?
Keep a list of starters on one page. Choose one in two minutes when you plan.

b: Teacher talks for five minutes about the topic: not a good starter.
Students match five words to pictures in pairs: good.
Teacher asks 'What did we do yesterday?' and waits in silence: weak.
A quick quiz with three questions on last week's grammar: good.

sections.h: Twelve starters you can use tomorrow
p: Here are twelve starters. Each one is quick and needs little material.
• 1. Word race: write as many words as possible on a topic in one minute (for example, kinds of homes).
• 2. Odd one out: show four words. Which does not belong? Students explain.
• 3. True or false: three statements about last lesson. Students decide and correct the false ones.
• 4. Picture prompt: show a picture. Students write five questions about it.
• 5. Quick-fire questions: ask five personal questions fast, students answer with a full sentence.
• 6. Jumbled sentence: write the words in the wrong order; students put them right.
• 7. Mini dictation: read two sentences slowly; students write them; pairs check.
• 8. Two truths and a lie: students write three sentences about themselves; partner guesses the lie.
• 9. Spelling relay: teams send one student at a time to write a word on the board.
• 10. One-minute talk: students talk to a partner on a simple topic without stopping.
• 11. Error hunt: write a sentence with one mistake from last lesson; students find it.
• 12. Question of the day: a big question on the board; students write one sentence answer and hold it up.

b: Speaking: 5, 8, 10, 12.
Writing: 1, 4, 6, 7.
Reading and vocabulary: 2, 9.
Review: 3, 11.

p: A plenary ends the lesson. It shows what students can now do. Here are ten plenaries.
• 1. Exit ticket: each student writes one thing they learned and one question on a slip of paper.
• 2. 3-2-1: three things I learned, two things I liked, one question.
• 3. Traffic lights: students hold up green, amber or red for the objective.
• 4. One sentence: write one sentence using today's language.
• 5. Teach your partner: explain one thing from today in 30 seconds.
• 6. Quick quiz: five questions on mini whiteboards or scrap paper.
• 7. Muddiest point: write the part that is still not clear.
• 8. Summary in ten words: students sum up the lesson in ten words.
• 9. Exam link: write one exam-style question about today's topic.
• 10. Self-check against success criteria: tick the criteria met.

ex.t: What to do with the slips
b: Sort them into three piles: got it, nearly, not yet.
Start tomorrow with a short review for the 'not yet' pile.
Keep a tally in your notebook.

p: Checking is not asking 'Do you understand?' Students nearly always say yes, even when they do not.
Use these tools:
• Concept checking questions (CCQs): simple questions that test meaning. For 'although', ask: 'Is it a reason or a contrast?'
• Instruction checking questions (ICQs): ask 'What do you do first?' after you give instructions.
• Mini whiteboards or paper: all students write an answer and hold it up together.
• Show with fingers: choose 1, 2 or 3.
• Wait time: after a question, wait three to five seconds before you choose someone. More students think.
• Ask students to explain to a partner before answering the class.
• Cold calling: choose a student by name after the question, not before, so everyone thinks.

b: Word: 'unusual'. Is it common or not common? Give an example.
Structure: 'I used to play football.' Do I play now?
Instruction: 'Work in pairs. One speaks, one listens.' Who speaks first?

p: A check is useful only if you act on it. Make a habit of three small steps.
• Note: write a quick note after each lesson. For example: 'Class 10B. Most used because correctly. Five students mix up take place and take part.'
• Adjust: change tomorrow's starter or first task to deal with the problem.
• Share: tell the students what you learned from their work. Say 'Most of you can... Some of you need...'.
Keep a one-page tracker for each class with the objective and a tick, a half-tick or a cross. At the end of the month you will see patterns.

b: Date | Objective | Evidence | Next step.
Example: 12 March | Use 'because' to give a reason | 20 of 28 students did it | Practise in the starter on Friday.

p: Vocabulary is a big part of the language marks in writing and speaking. Students must use a range of common and less common words. Words are forgotten quickly unless they come back many times.
Try these routines:
• Five new words per lesson, not more. Teach them in a sentence, not alone.
• Teach collocations: words that go together, such as 'make a decision', 'heavy rain', 'take part in'.
• Word families: teach 'decide, decision, decisive'.
• Word notebooks: students write the word, a sentence, the meaning and a translation if they need it.
• Spaced review: revisit new words after one day, one week and one month.
• Use words in speaking and writing tasks the same week.
Common words the examiner report says students mix up: 'take place' and 'take part'. Teach pairs like these together with examples.

b: Monday: teach five words.
Tuesday: starter quiz on the words.
Next Monday: use them in a short writing task.
One month later: a mixed review.

activity: Choose three starters and three plenaries from this unit. Write them into your next week's plans. After the lessons note which ones worked best and why.

check.q: Which question best checks that students understand how to start a pair task?
What should you do with exit tickets?
o: Sort them and plan the next lesson from them
Throw them away after the lesson
Mark every one with a grade
Read them only at the end of term

check.q: Which review pattern helps students remember new words?
o: After one day, one week and one month
Only once at the end of the year
Only on the day they are taught

title: Integrating Skills: From Input to Output
summary: Learn how to join reading and listening to writing and speaking in one sequence, with four patterns, worked examples from the 2024 specimen paper and a weekly planning grid.

p: Receptive skills are reading and listening. Students take in language. Productive skills are writing and speaking. Students make language.

In the real world, we rarely use just one skill. We read an email and reply. We listen to a talk and discuss it. The Cambridge exam follows this idea. The papers test each skill alone, but the topics are real and the tasks link to real life.
When you link skills in one lesson sequence:
• Students have ideas and words to use when they speak or write.
• They see how language works in a real text first, then use it.
• They practise the same words and structures many times.
• You save time, because one topic serves four skills.
Without input, students often have nothing to say or write. Without output, they only recognise language and cannot use it.

b: Input first, then notice, then practise, then produce.
Always end with an output task.

sections.h: The skills chain: input, noticing, practice, output
p: Use this chain to plan a sequence of one to four lessons.
• Input: students read a text or listen to a recording. The first task is about meaning only. For example: What is the main idea?
• Noticing: students look closely at the language. Which words and phrases help? How is the text organised?
• Practice: students use the key language in controlled tasks with a correct answer.
• Output: students speak or write on a new but related topic, using the language they noticed.
• Feedback and redo: the teacher gives feedback and students try again.

img.alt: A diagram showing four steps in a row: input, noticing, practice, output, with an arrow back to feedback
img.cap: The skills chain. Input leads to noticing, practice and output. Feedback closes the loop.

b: Does the sequence start with input?
Is there a pause to notice language?
Do students get to produce something of their own?
Is there time for feedback and a second try?

sections.h: Pattern 1: Reading, then speaking, then writing
p: Here is an example using the reading text from the 2024 specimen Paper 1. The article, All about living stone plants, is about plants that look like small stones. It uses words such as resemble, tap root, container, sandy soil and protect.

Lesson A (reading). Students answer Exercise 1 questions. They find facts: where the plants grow, what the head is, how tall they are, what advice the writer gives. Task: underline the advice sentences.

Noticing. Look at how the text gives advice: 'it is best to grow them in sandy soil', 'it is important to protect the plants', 'it is essential to be patient'. These are patterns: it is + adjective + to + verb.
Lesson B (speaking). Pairs give advice about a plant or pet using the same pattern. Then a one-minute talk: 'Tell me about an animal or plant in your area and how to look after it.'
Lesson C (writing). Write an informal email to a friend who wants to grow a plant. Give three pieces of advice. 120 to 160 words.
Result: one text supports reading, speaking and writing, and students practise a useful structure in all three.

b: Take any short text from a past paper.
Pick one language pattern in it.
Plan one speaking task and one writing task that use the pattern.

sections.h: Pattern 2: Listening, then speaking, then writing
p: Pick a recording on a topic of the unit. It can be a Paper 2 extract, or a short recording you make yourself with a colleague.
Step 1: Listen for gist. What is it about? Who is speaking?
Step 2: Listen again for detail. Fill in a table or notes.
Step 3: Notice useful phrases. For example 'I'd rather', 'What I like about it is', 'In my opinion'.
Step 4: Speak. Pairs give their own opinion on the same topic using two of the phrases.
Step 5: Write. Students write a short summary or an email to a friend about what they heard and what they think.

Tip for Paper 2: after the exam practice, replay the recording with the script. Students see where the answers were and which words were distractors. The examiner report says many students pick the word they hear in the recording instead of the idea.

b: Recording: 'I suddenly heard a bang in the engine.'
Correct option: 'It made a loud noise.'
Many students did not link the two ideas.
Class task: match recording sentences to option sentences with different words.

p: Speaking can prepare writing. Talk first, write second. Students who have said their ideas aloud write more and with less fear.
Example: Paper 3 Part 2 card, 'School newspaper'. Students prepare for one minute, talk for two minutes in pairs about which article they would prefer to write and why.

Then switch to writing: write a short article or review about the same topic for the school newspaper. Use ideas from the talk. Students can listen to a partner's talk and take notes, then write an email to a friend about what the partner said.
This pattern also helps students who think they have nothing to write. They already said it.

b: Talk for one minute with a partner.
Write three key ideas from the talk.
Write a paragraph for each idea.

sections.h: Pattern 4: Reading two texts, then writing a report
p: Exercise 6 asks for a more formal piece, such as a report, article, review or essay. Students need ideas and a formal register. One good way is to give them two short texts with different views.
Step 1: Read text A (advantages) and text B (disadvantages). Underline key ideas.
Step 2: Notice formal phrases: 'It is clear that', 'However', 'On the other hand', 'In conclusion'.
Step 3: Plan: introduction, two paragraphs, a conclusion and a recommendation.
Step 4: Write 120 to 160 words, using ideas from the texts and one idea of your own.
Examiner reports remind us that students who only copy the prompts score lower for Content. They must develop prompts or add their own ideas.

b: The aim of this report is to...
One enjoyable part was...
However, there were some problems...
I would recommend that...

sections.h: A weekly planning grid for integrated skills
p: Use a grid to plan the week around one theme. Here is an example for the theme 'Travel'.
• Lesson 1: Reading. A short article on a travel problem. Exercise 1 and Exercise 3 skills. Notice linking words.
• Lesson 2: Listening. Two short travel stories. Exercise 2 style. Notice phrases for opinions.
• Lesson 3: Speaking. A Part 2 style card: a train journey or a bus journey. Talk for two minutes. Peer feedback.
• Lesson 4: Writing. An email to a friend about a journey, 120 to 160 words, using ideas and phrases from Lessons 1 to 3. Feedback and redo.
Check: in four lessons you practised all four skills, used the same topic words and finished with one piece of real output.

b: Too much input and no time for output.
Skills that are not connected to the same topic.
Giving the same task every week.
No feedback loop, so students repeat the same mistakes.

activity: Plan a four-lesson sequence for one theme from your scheme. Name the input text or audio, the language to notice, one speaking task and one writing task. Show the plan to a colleague and ask: Does one lesson lead naturally to the next?

check.q: What is the correct order in the skills chain?
Why does the examiner report warn about copying the prompts in a report?
o: Content marks are higher when ideas are developed or added
Prompts are not allowed in the exam
Copying makes the report too long

title: Teaching with Past Papers and the Specimen Paper
summary: Use past papers and the 2024 specimen Paper 1 in lessons, with the full structure of the specimen paper, its answers and practical three-lesson sequences for each exercise.

sections.h: When and how to use past papers
p: Past papers are the best practice for the exam because the questions match the real style. But they are not the best first step. Use them in stages.
• Stage 1: Learn the task. Look at one exercise, learn what it asks, practise the skill with easier texts.
• Stage 2: Practise by exercise. Do one exercise at a time with time limits.
• Stage 3: Timed full paper. Do a whole paper under exam rules, once or twice a term.
• Stage 4: Review and redo. Go through the mark scheme, find errors and try again.
Do not give a past paper every week from the start. Students become afraid, and teachers miss the chance to build skills. Use mock exams at the end of modules and in the final term.
Keep the real mark scheme. After every attempt, ask students to mark their own or a partner's work with the mark scheme. This is excellent training.

b: June 2024 papers and mark schemes (download).
The 2024 specimen Paper 1 and mark scheme (download).
Older papers for your syllabus period: ask the School Support Hub.
Never share live exam papers or confidential materials.

p: The specimen paper shows the structure for examination from 2024. It has 17 questions and 60 marks. Use it to explain the paper to students.
• Exercise 1 (Questions 1 to 6, 8 marks). A short article, All about living stone plants. Five one-mark questions and one three-mark question (advice).
• Exercise 2 (Question 7(a) to (i), 9 marks). A matching task with nine statements.
• Exercise 3 (Questions 8 and 9, 7 marks). Notes under two headings about tiny homes: three marks for disadvantages and four marks for reasons they are popular.
• Exercise 4 (Questions 10 to 15, 6 marks). Six multiple-choice questions, three options each.
• Exercise 5 (Question 16, 15 marks). An informal email to a friend about a problem with an item bought online. Three bullet points. About 120 to 160 words. 6 marks Content, 9 marks Language.

• Exercise 6 (Question 17, 15 marks). A report about a sports festival, using speech-bubble comments as ideas and also some ideas of your own. About 120 to 160 words. 6 marks Content, 9 marks Language.

b: Reading: 8 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 30 marks.
Writing: 15 + 15 = 30 marks.
Total: 60 marks.

sections.h: The specimen answers, and how to teach from them
p: Here are the answers from the specimen mark scheme, with teaching ideas.

Exercise 1. Q1 South Africa. Q2 (the) head. Q3 prevents insect attacks. Q4 mist. Q5 two centimetres. Q6, any three of: grow them in sandy soil, protect the plants from strong sunlight, use a container of sufficient depth, be patient.
Teaching idea: ask students to highlight the key word in each question before they read ('country', 'pair of leaves', 'protect', 'main source of water', 'how tall'). Then let them find the sentence.

Exercise 2. Q7: (a) C, (b) A, (c) D, (d) B, (e) C, (f) D, (g) B, (h) A, (i) D. Teaching idea: students underline the key words in the statement, then find the idea in the texts. They must find paraphrase, not the same word.

Exercise 3. Q8 disadvantages of tiny homes, any three: high cost of the fuel needed to transport them; not every region has building regulations; not always straightforward to connect to a range of services; can be tricky to control the temperature inside. Q9 reasons why they are popular, any four: can be easily moved; encourages you to get rid of unnecessary possessions; increased media interest in the idea; many companies now specialise in building them; desire to leave a smaller carbon footprint.
Teaching idea: notes should be short and under the right heading. Practise by sorting notes into 'disadvantages' and 'reasons for popularity'.
Exercise 4. Q10 A, Q11 C, Q12 B, Q13 A, Q14 B, Q15 B. Teaching idea: for each option, ask students to find the sentence in the text that matches or rejects it. Only one fully answers the question.

b: Brackets in the mark scheme mean the words are not essential.
One mark for each acceptable detail up to the maximum.
Spelling errors in reading answers do not lose marks if the meaning is clear and unambiguous.
Marks are never taken away for errors or for omissions.

p: Exercise 5, Question 16. The task: You recently bought an item online. There was a problem with it. Write an email to a friend about the problem. In your email you should explain why you bought the item, describe the problem with the item and say what you are going to do about it. Write about 120 to 160 words.

Use the three bullets as a plan: paragraph 1 why I bought it, paragraph 2 the problem, paragraph 3 what I will do. Add a greeting and a friendly ending. Use informal language: contractions, exclamations, questions to the reader.

Exercise 6, Question 17. The task: Your class took part in a one-day sports festival. The organisers want students' opinions. Write a report saying what was enjoyable and suggesting how it could be improved. Comments from students: 'It was a chance to meet students from other schools', 'There weren't many new sports to try', 'I learned a lot about fitness', 'We spent too much time listening to instructions.'

Plan: introduction (aim of the report), what was enjoyable, what could be improved with suggestions, a conclusion. Use a formal or semi-formal style. Use some of the comments and add ideas of your own.
Both tasks are marked with Table A (Content, 6 marks) and Table B (Language, 9 marks), which you studied in Week 2.

b: Address all three bullets in Exercise 5 to reach the higher marks.
In Exercise 6, extend or add to the prompts.
Keep the register right: friendly for the email, formal for the report.
Do not confuse 'take place' with 'take part'.

sections.h: A three-lesson sequence for one exercise
p: Use this pattern for any exercise.
Lesson A: Learn the task.
• Show the exercise. Ask: What do I have to do? How many marks? How long should I take?
• Do a similar short task with an easier text together.
• Teach the strategy (for example, underline key words, find paraphrase).
Lesson B: Practise.
• Students do the real exercise in a set time, alone.
• Mark in pairs with the mark scheme.
• Collect common errors.
Lesson C: Review and redo.
• Talk through the hard questions and why wrong options look good.
• Students correct errors and write an error log.
• A short second attempt on a new text or new question.

b: Question number | My answer | Correct answer | Why I got it wrong | What I will do next time.
Review the log before the next mock exam.

p: A full mock gives you and your students real information.
• Plan the date in your calendar.
• Use a quiet room, desks apart, no dictionaries, clock visible.
• Give instructions exactly as in the exam: read the instructions, do all questions, write on the paper.
• Time it. Paper 1 takes 2 hours.
• Mark all papers using the mark scheme. Use the Content and Language tables for writing.
• Give feedback within a week. If you wait a month, the lesson is lost.
After the mock, plan three lessons for the three most common problems. Do not move on to a new topic before you reteach.
Balance: past papers should be only part of your course. Keep using texts and recordings from outside the exam too, so students read and listen for real.

b: Group the common errors.
Reteach in a new starter or a small-group lesson.
Praise students who improved.
Set one target for each student.

activity: Choose one exercise from the 2024 specimen paper or a June 2024 paper. Plan a three-lesson sequence (learn, practise, review). Write the strategy you will teach, the time limit, how students will mark and what the error log looks like.

title: My Learning Tracker: Week 4 KWL Chart and Lesson Portfolio
summary: Update your KWL chart for Week 4, reflect on how your planning has changed, check your lesson plan portfolio and look ahead to Week 5.

p: Open your KWL chart. Update the L column for Week 4. Write at least two specific things you learned about lesson planning and skills.
Be exact. Instead of 'I learned about lessons', write 'I learned that a 55 minute lesson needs a starter, three main phases and a plenary, and the plenary should never be cut'.
Then look at your W column. Did this week answer some of your questions? Cross them out and write the answer. Add new questions.

b: Learned: write lesson objectives with a verb students can show.
Learned: start with input, then notice, then practise, then produce.
Learned: use the mark scheme with students after a past paper.
Question: how do I run a speaking mock for a class of 40?

p: A portfolio is a folder of your best planning. It shows your growth and helps your colleagues. At the end of Week 4 you should have:
• One four-column scheme of work for two weeks or more.
• One full 55 minute lesson plan with timings.
• A bank of starters and plenaries you will use.
• One integrated skills sequence with reading, speaking and writing.
• One three-lesson sequence with a past paper exercise.
• A tracker for one class.
If any item is missing, go back to the unit and finish it. These are the tools you will use every week.

b: Is every item dated?
Is each lesson plan realistic for my class?
Have I written what I would change?

sections.h: Try your plan with a colleague
p: Plans are better when someone else reads them. Ask a colleague to read your lesson plan and answer three questions.
• Could I teach from this?
• What will the students be doing in minute 20?
• How will you know if the objective was reached?

If possible, invite the colleague to observe part of the lesson. After the lesson, talk for 10 minutes. Start with what went well. Then choose one thing to change. Observation is not a test. It is a way for both teachers to learn.

b: Time | What students were doing | What I noticed.
Write facts, not opinions.

p: Next week you will go deeper into how you teach. You will learn about communicative language teaching and task-based learning. You will also learn how to make your own reading, writing and speaking tasks, and how to adapt textbooks and create simple checklists for students.
Before you start Week 5:
• Try one new starter and one new plenary this week.
• Write down one problem you want help with, such as shy students or large classes.
• Collect one real text from a newspaper, website or school notice board that you could use for a worksheet.

b: Teach one lesson using your new plan.
Record what happened.
Bring the real text to Week 5.

activity: Write your Week 4 L entries (at least two specific things), answer any W questions now solved, add new questions, and write three sentences on how your lesson planning has changed. Update your portfolio list.
